paragraphs.text: AHMAD NADEEM ARSHAD, J:- Through the instant civil revision petition, the petitioner has called in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 20.05.2014, passed by the learned Civil Judge, Ferozwala, whereby an application filed by the petitioner under Section 12(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as "the C.P.C.") was rejected by invoking the provisions of Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., on the ground of being barred by limitation.

Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to the instant petition are that respondent No.1 instituted a suit for specific performance against respondent No.2, seeking enforcement of an agreement to sell dated 10.04.1987. The said suit culminated in a judgment and decree dated 03.10.1995, whereby the learned trial Court decreed the suit in favour of respondent No.1. Feeling aggrieved, the petitioner approached the learned trial Court by filing an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., assailing the validity of the aforesaid judgment and decree. The application was contested by the respondents. During its pendency, respondent No.1 moved an application under Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., seeking rejection of the petitioner's application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., on the plea that the same was barred by limitation. The learned trial Court, after obtaining a reply thereto, allowed the application filed by respondent No.1 and, vide the impugned order dated 20.05.2014, rejected the petitioner's application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., as time- barred. Hence, the present civil revision petition.

The record reflects that respondent No.1 was duly served through her Manager, as evidenced by the report of the Process Server dated 27.11.2014, and that a Power of Attorney/Vakalatnama on her behalf was filed by Ch. Ahmed Raza Chatha, Advocate. Likewise, the legal heirs of respondent No.2 were served through their Manager, Saif Ullah, as borne out by the report of the Process Server dated 26.11.2014. However, despite repeated calls, no one appeared on behalf of the respondents to contest the proceedings. Consequently, the respondents are proceeded against exparte.

The controversy requiring determination in the present proceedings is whether an application instituted under Section 12(2), C.P.C., can lawfully be rejected by resorting to the provisions of Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., which, by its express language and statutory scheme, deals with rejection of a plaint. In order to appreciate the controversy, it would be advantageous to reproduce the relevant provision of Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., which reads as under: "11. Rejection of plaint.—The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:— (a) where it does not disclose a cause of action; (b) where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so; (c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so; and (d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law." A plain reading of the above provision makes it abundantly clear that the legislature has employed the expression "plaint" throughout the rule and has confined its application to the circumstances specifically enumerated therein. The provision is directed towards the scrutiny of a plaint presented for the institution of a civil suit and empowers the Court to reject such plaint where any of the statutory conditions stipulated in clauses (a) to (d) is attracted. The expression "plaint" cannot, by any stretch of statutory interpretation, be equated with every application, petition or miscellaneous proceeding instituted before a civil Court. Had the legislature intended to extend the operation of Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., to applications of every description, it would have employed language sufficiently comprehensive to encompass such proceedings. The absence of such language is significant and cannot be supplied by judicial interpretation.

It is equally relevant to observe that Order VII of the C.P.C. is captioned "Plaint" and Rule 1 thereof prescribes the particulars which a plaint is required to contain. A plaint is the foundational pleading through which a civil suit is instituted, whereas an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., is a distinct statutory proceeding seeking adjudication of the validity of an already pronounced judgment, decree or order. The two proceedings are different in their nature, character, purpose and procedural framework. Consequently, an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., cannot be converted into a plaint merely because it seeks substantive relief against an existing judgment, order or decree.

In this regard, Section 12(2), C.P.C., assumes considerable significance. The said provision reads as follows: "12(2). Where a person challenges the validity of a judgment, decree or order on the plea of fraud, mis- representation or want of jurisdiction, he shall seek his remedy by making an application to the Court which passed the final judgment, decree or order and not by a separate suit." The legislative intent underlying the aforesaid provision is manifest. It provides a specific and self-contained procedural remedy to an aggrieved person who seeks to impeach the validity of a judgment, decree or order on the grounds of fraud, misrepresentation or want of jurisdiction. Instead of permitting the institution of an independent suit for such purpose, the legislature has directed the aggrieved person to approach the Court which passed the final judgment, decree or order by means of an application. The remedy, therefore, is not a fresh civil suit but a statutory application to be adjudicated in accordance with the provisions of Section 12(2), C.P.C.

Once the legislature has expressly prescribed the mode through which such a challenge is to be brought before the Court, the nature of the proceeding must be determined in accordance with the provision under which it is instituted and the relief sought therein. The nomenclature and substance of the proceeding cannot be disregarded so as to attract a procedural provision which is otherwise confined to a different class of proceedings. An application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., thus, remains an application notwithstanding the fact that it seeks to set aside an existing judgment, decree or order.

The controversy is no longer a new matter. The Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, in the case of “Salah-ud-Din v. Mst. Zia Farhat” (1996 SCMR 1528), while examining an analogous controversy, considered whether an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., could be treated as a plaint within the contemplation of Order VII, Rule 1, C.P.C., and consequently be rejected under Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C. The Hon’ble Supreme Court observed that it was doubtful whether an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., constituted a plaint within the meaning of Order VII, Rule 1, C.P.C., or could be dismissed under Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., on the grounds advanced by the applicant seeking its rejection. The Hon’ble Supreme Court declined interference with the interlocutory orders passed by the Courts below and refused leave to appeal.

The aforesaid dictum was subsequently considered and elaborated by this Court in “Maula Bakhsh v. Muhammad Hussain and others” (PLD 2013 Lahore 51). This Court, after examining the relevant statutory provisions and the dictum of the Hon;ble Supreme Court in Salah-ud-Din's case (supra), held in unequivocal terms that an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., could not be treated as a plaint within the meaning of Order VII, Rule 1, C.P.C., and, therefore, could not be rejected under Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C. The relevant observation made therein is reproduced below: "Now the question surfaces on the scene is that when the petition was not maintainable before the trial court whether it was obliged to reject the same under Order VII Rule 11 C.P.C. In this regard, I am of the humble opinion that the application under section 12(2), C.P.C. cannot be treated as plaint within the meaning of Order VII Rule 1 C.P.C., thus, the court is not empowered reject the same under Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C." The august Supreme Court of Pakistan in another judgment reported as “Mrs. ANIS HAIDER and others versus S. AMIR HAIDER and others” (2008 SCMR 236) while dealing with a matter wherein an application under section 12(2) C.P.C. was rejected under Order VII Rule 11, C.P.C. by the learned trial court and upheld up to this Court converted the petition into appeal and by accepting the same remanded the matter to the learned trial court for decision of the application under section 12(2), C.P.C. afresh after recording evidence of both the parties. It was held as under:- “10. The very terminology used in Order VII, rule 11, C.P.C. is indicative of the fact that it pertains to suits and plaints in particular. The Court should have realized the difference between a regular suit and an application. Section 141, C.P.C. cannot be attracted as it pertains to the ordinary procedure laid down in Civil Procedure Code that may be followed in deciding an application but a substantial requirement of recording of evidence on pure and serious question of fact could not be by-passed by unjustifiable invoking of Order VII, rule 11, C.P.C. It appears that even the implication of Order VII, rule 11, C.P.C. were not properly appreciated and applied. The order can be attracted only when a plaint by itself does not disclose any cause of action. It cannot be rejected on the basis of written statement because the initial burden remains on the plaintiff/petitioner to prove his case on the basis of assertions made in the pleadings. If the principle in hand adopted by the Courts below is endorsed, it would be the easiest thing to dismiss any civil suit simply and merely on the basis of written statement.” The aforesaid legal proposition is founded upon a sound interpretation of the statutory scheme and is fully consonant with the dictum of the august Supreme Court. It is settled that where a statute prescribes a particular procedure for the exercise of a judicial remedy, such procedure must be adhered to, and a provision governing a different class of proceedings cannot be pressed into service merely to achieve a procedural result which may otherwise appear convenient. The jurisdiction of a Court must be exercised within the confines of the authority conferred upon it by law. A procedural provision cannot be enlarged beyond its permissible scope so as to encompass proceedings which the legislature has not brought within its ambit.

There is, however, an important distinction between the applicability of Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., and the question whether an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., is barred by limitation. The fact that Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., is not attracted to an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., does not confer immunity upon such application from the law of limitation. An application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., is undoubtedly subject to the applicable law of limitation, and its competence must be examined in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Limitation Act, 1908. However, the existence of a limitation bar does not, by itself, enlarge the scope of Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., or transform an application into a plaint. In this context, the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, in “Government of Sindh and another v. Ch. Fazal Muhammad” (PLD 1991 Supreme Court 197), examined the question of limitation governing applications under Section 12(2), C.P.C., and held that, in the absence of a specific period of limitation prescribed for such applications, the residuary Article 181 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908, would apply, prescribing a period of three years from the date when the right to apply accrues. The judgment further explained the relationship between the statutory remedy under Section 12(2), C.P.C., and the corresponding provisions of the Limitation Act. The aforesaid principle was reiterated by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in “Bashir Ahmed through Legal Representatives and others v. Muhammad Hussain and others” (PLD 2019 Supreme Court 504). The Hon;ble Supreme Court held that an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., is governed by Article 181 of the Limitation Act, 1908, and the prescribed period is three years from the date when the right to apply accrues. Where an applicant asserts that fraud or concealment prevented him from acquiring knowledge of the impugned judgment, decree or order, Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1908, may become relevant for determining the commencement of limitation. The Court further emphasized that allegations of fraud or concealment must be specifically pleaded with requisite particulars and cannot rest upon vague or general assertions.

The aforesaid case law, therefore, establish two distinct legal propositions: firstly, an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., is amenable to the law of limitation; and secondly, its rejection cannot be ordered by mechanically invoking Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C., as though it were a plaint. The former concerns the substantive competence of the application, whereas the latter concerns the procedural jurisdiction and statutory authority under which the Court is empowered to pass an order. These two questions cannot be conflated. Applying the said principles to the facts of the present case, it is evident that the petitioner had invoked the jurisdiction of the learned trial Court by filing an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., challenging the validity of the judgment and decree in question. The said proceeding was, by its very nature, a statutory application and not a plaint instituting a fresh civil suit. Respondent No.1, instead of seeking determination of the question of limitation through the procedure legally applicable to such an application, invoked Order VII, Rule 11, C.P.C. The learned trial Court, while entertaining the said application, failed to appreciate the fundamental distinction between a plaint and an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., and proceeded to reject the latter by resorting to a provision which was not attracted to the proceedings before it.

The impugned order, therefore, suffers from a patent legal infirmity. The learned trial Court has exercised its jurisdiction by applying a procedural provision beyond the scope contemplated by the legislature. Such an approach cannot be sustained in the eyes of law, particularly when the precise controversy stands addressed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Salah-ud-Din's case (supra), Mrs. Anis Haider case (supra) and has subsequently been elaborated by this Court in Maula Bakhsh's case (supra). It is clarified, however, that the setting aside of the impugned order shall not be construed as an expression of opinion on the merits or maintainability of the petitioner's application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., nor shall it be taken to mean that the said application is necessarily within limitation. The question of limitation, including the applicability of Article 181 and, where properly pleaded and established, Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1908, shall remain open to be determined by the learned trial Court in accordance with law, after affording the parties an opportunity of hearing and examining the relevant pleadings, material and circumstances. The petitioner shall also be required to establish the necessary particulars of the alleged fraud, misrepresentation or want of jurisdiction, as contemplated by Section 12(2), C.P.C.

For what has been discussed above, the instant civil revision petition is accepted. Consequently, the impugned order dated 20.05.2014, passed by the learned Civil Judge, Ferozwala, is set-aside. The matter is remanded to the learned trial Court for decision of the petitioner's application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., afresh, strictly in accordance with law and in the light of the observations made hereinabove. The learned trial Court shall independently determine all questions relating to the maintainability and limitation of the application, without being influenced by any observation in this judgment touching upon the merits of the controversy. The parties are directed to appear before the learned District Judge, Sheikhupura, on 21.11.2026, who shall entrust the matter to any civil Court of competent jurisdiction at Tehsil Ferozwala. No order as to costs. (AHMAD NADEEM ARSHAD) JUDGE Approved for reporting. JUDGE Gull*
